# Part 1

## 1.1 Introduction

The dataset, 'housing', contains the predictors 'size_sqft', 'bedrooms', and 'age_years'
and the response variable 'price_thousands'. The goal is to fit and diagnose a linear model
that models the price of houses based on the three predictors using matrix computation.

# Part 2

``` {python}
predictors = df[["size_sqft", "bedrooms", "age_years"]].to_numpy()
y = df["price_thousands"].to_numpy()
```

### Standardize the Predictors

``` {python}
means = predictors.mean(axis=0)
sds = predictors.std(axis=0)

Z = (predictors- means) / sds
```

``` {python}
Z.mean(axis=0)
```

``` {python}
Z.std(axis=0)
```

Mean across the predictors = `{python} f"{Z.mean(axis=0)[0]:.2f}"`,
`{python} f"{Z.mean(axis=0)[1]:.2f}"`, `{python} f"{Z.mean(axis=0)[2]:.2f}"`

Standard deviation across the predictors: `{python} f"{Z.std(axis=0)[0]:.2f}"`,
`{python} f"{Z.std(axis=0)[1]:.2f}"`, `{python} f"{Z.std(axis=0)[2]:.2f}"`

### Construct the Design matrix

``` {python}
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(Z)), Z])
```

The 'predictors' array (an array containing the values of each of the three explanatory variables
for each observation) has `{python} predictors.shape[1]` columns (predictors) and `{python} predictors.shape[0]`
rows (observations) (`{python} predictors.shape`).

``` {python}
predictors.shape
```

The 'Z' array (an array containing the Z-scores of each explanatory variable for each observation)
that also has `{python} Z.shape[1]` columns and `{python} Z.shape[0]` rows (`{python} Z.shape`).

``` {python}
Z.shape
```

The 'X' array (an array that acts as the design matrix for the computations) has `{python} X.shape[1]`
 columns and `{python} X.shape[0]` rows (`{python} X.shape`). The extra column is an intercept columns
 that only contains 1s.

``` {python}
X.shape
```

The 'y' array (an array with the response values (price in thousands) for each observation) is
1-dimensional with `{python} y.shape[0]` entries (`{python} y.shape`).

``` {python}
y.shape
```

The matrix rank of X is `{python} f"{np.linalg.matrix_rank(X)}"`.

``` {python}
np.linalg.matrix_rank(X)
```

There are three predictors excluding the intercept. This is clear when looking at the number of
dimensions of 'predictors'.

``` {python}
predictors.shape
```

## Written Response

X and y must have compatable shapes because each row of X holds one observation's predictors and
each entry of y is that observation's response, so X and y need the same number of rows in order
to produce one fitted value per observation. The intercept column is necessary
in X because X will be multiplied (as a matrix) by the beta matrix which includes the intercept
beta (beta0) which estimates the average response when every predictor is at its mean. Standardizing
the predictors puts all the predictors on a common, comparable scale without
altering their relationship to the response or their distribution. Broadcasting allows the code
to complete element-wise subtraction of the mean from the predictor values (predictor - mean) and
division of the standard deviation (/ sds) in order to complete the same calculations without a
loop.

# Part 3

### Fit the Model

``` {python}
beta_hat, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond = None)
```

``` {python}
beta_hat
```

Estimated Coefficients:
Intercept coefficient = `{python} f"{beta_hat[0].2f}"`

size_sqft coefficient = `{python} f"{beta_hat[1].2f}"`

bedrooms coefficient = `{python} f"{beta_hat[2].2f}"`

age_years coefficient = `{python} f"{beta_hat[3].2f}"`

size_sqft has the largest absolute value coefficient (`{python} f"{beta_hat[1].2f}"`).

### Calculate Fitted Values and Residuals

``` {python}
fitted = X @ beta_hat
residuals = y- fitted
rmse = np.sqrt(np.mean(residuals ** 2))
```

``` {python}
rmse
```

``` {python}
residuals.mean()
```

The RMSE is `{python} f"{rmse:.3f}"` and the residual mean is `{python} f"{residuals.mean():.2e}"`.

## Written Response

X @ beta_hat is matrix multiplication that calculates the dot of each row of X and the beta_hat
coefficients, and it
represents the predicted outcome for each observation based on the estimated beta values
and the observation's predictor values. The residual mean should be near zero when an intercept is
present because least squares with an intercept forces residuals to be orthogonal to the column of ones.
RMSE summarizes how far a model’s predictions are from the actual observed response values, on average.
X * beta_hat uses element-wise multiplication that broadcasts beta_hat across columns of X
while X @ beta_hat uses matrix multiplication.

# Part 4

## QR Decomposition

``` {python}
Q, R = np.linalg.qr(X)
```

Q has `{python} Q.shape[1]' columns and `{python} Q.shape[0]` rows (`{python} Q.shape`)
while R is a square matrix with `{python} R.shape[1]` columns and `{python} R.shape[0]` rows
(`{python} R.shape`).

``` {python}
Q.shape
```

``` {python}
R.shape
```

Multiplying Q and R results in the design matrix (X), and the columns of Q are orthogonal.

``` {python}
np.allclose(Q @ R, X)
```

``` {python}
np.allclose(Q.T @ Q, np.eye(Q.shape[1]))
```

## SVD

``` {python}
U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(X, full_matrices=False)
```

U has `{python} U.shape` columns and `{python} U.shape[0]` rows (`{python} U.shape`),
s is a 1-dimentional array with `{python} s.shape[0]` singular values (`{python} s.shape`),
and Vt has `{python} Vt.shape[1]` columns and `{python} Vt.shape[0]` rows (`{python} Vt.shape`).

``` {python}
U.shape
```

``` {python}
s.shape
```

``` {python}
Vt.shape
```

The singular values are `{python} f"{s[0].2f}"`, `{python} f"{s[1].2f}"`, `{python} f"{s[2].2f}"`,
and `{python} f"{s[3].2f}"`.

``` {python}
s
```

``` {python}
X_reconstructed = (U @ np.diag(s) @ Vt)
```

The reconstructed design matrix (reconstructed X) is similar to the original design matrix (X)
that was created in Part 2.

``` {python}
np.allclose(X_reconstructed, X)
```

## Rank and Conditioning

The rank of the design matrix (X) is `{python} f"{np.linalg.matrix_rank(X)}"`. The largest
singular value is about `{python} f"{np.linalg.cond(X).2f}"` times the smallest which
means that the design matrix (X) is well conditioned.

``` {python}
np.linalg.cond(X)
```

``` {python}
X_raw = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(predictors)), predictors])
```

The largest singular value of the raw design matrix (raw X) is about
`{python} f"{np.linalg.cond(X_raw).2f}"` times the smallest which means that the raw
design matric (raw X) is not well conditioned.

``` {python}
np.linalg.cond(X_raw)
```

## Written Response

Q @ R ≈ X verifies that Q and R really are a decomposition of X, and Q.T @ Q ≈ I verifies that
the dimensions of Q are orthogonal. Each singular value measures how much the design matrix (X)
stretched the input in one direction. A large condition number suggests that the design matrix is
not well conditioned because X stretches by a different amount in each direction. The condition
number did change after standardization. Mismatched measurement scales can inflate the raw
condition number because singular values are based on each column/dimension's units. Because the
condition number of the standardized design matrix was low
(`{python} f"{np.linalg.cond(X).2f}"`), it does not show evidence of severe redundancy
among predictors.

# Part 5

Clean execution is necessary for a computational report because the code must run seamlessly
from top to bottom in order for the report to work properly. A properly ran report proves that
the results actually came from the code provided. Reusable code should not depend on hidden
notebook state because code can be ran out of order, and code can be altered without being ran
from top to bottom. As a result, some code can not be reproducible when ran chronologically.
Additionally, variables defined in a deleted or edited cell still exist in memory, so future code
can work only because of code that was previously written. The main reason why np.linalg.lstsq()
is preferred over manual computation is because manually computing inverse matrices takes up a
lot of time and can produce numerical error. The function np.linalg.lstsq() solves the
optimization without taking the time to calculate an inverse matrix which saves time and reduces
error. Using a check like np.allclose() is preferable to checking exact equality for QR and SVD
because rounded values could consider the deconstructed values to be different than the original
(not decontructed) values eventhough they are fundamentally equal. In my analysis, the raw matrix
had a very large condition number while the standardized one was reasonable. The condition number
comparison taught me that numerical data can alter drastically when scale changes. It showed me
how important it is to explicitly state the scales of variables, so that the analysis can be
reproduced. I learned that making a detailed report is very useful for reproducibility because
the person coding is able to provide indepth details about each piece of code in order to tell
a story. To apply this to the final project, I will restart and run all cells before submitting
or making conclusions.
